planting.note: Sow over a lean mineral cactus mix in a warm propagation tray; seedlings are slow and benefit from bright shade until their first year of true spines develops.

directions: Native to the limestone hills of Coahuila and Nuevo Leon, this solitary Mexican species forms a broad, flattened, blue-gray globe divided into a handful of wide, low, angular ribs rather than the more numerous fine ribs typical of many barrel cacti. Long, flat, curving central spines lie against the body in a ribbon-like sweep, and in fall it produces large, satiny flowers in white to pale pink with a darker midstripe down each petal, opening wide in sun. It is distinguished from Thelocactus bicolor by its broader, more compressed body and muted gray-green coloring rather than a rounder, more strongly ribbed form. Grow in a fast-draining mineral substrate with strong light and minimal water, particularly through winter dormancy when the thick body is prone to rot if kept damp.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Sow into a gritty, low-organic mix and keep cool through the first winter, since this Colorado Plateau native expects a genuine cold dormancy to grow and flower well.

directions: Widespread across the sandy and rocky high deserts of Utah, Colorado, Arizona, and New Mexico, this small barrel-shaped cactus is one of the more cold-hardy globular species in cultivation, tolerating hard freezes and even snow cover in its native range. The body is armed with stout, strongly hooked central spines radiating from woolly areoles, giving rise to the common name, and in late spring it produces funnel-shaped flowers in pink to magenta clustered near the crown. Unlike the tender lowland fishhook cacti of Ferocactus and Echinocactus, it demands a true winter chill to trigger reliable flowering and resents warm, wet winters. Site it in raised, mineral-heavy soil in full sun with excellent drainage, and withhold water almost entirely from late fall through winter.

planting.note: Sow in a deep container to accommodate the developing tuberous root, and expect the thin, gray, easily overlooked stems to take several years before they are large enough to flower.

directions: Native to the Sonoran and Chihuahuan Deserts of Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, and northern Mexico, this cactus spends most of the year disguised as a dead, gray-brown, pencil-thin shrub, its thin ribbed stems scrambling unnoticed through the branches of creosote and mesquite. Below ground it stores water and energy in an enormous, turnip-like tuberous root that can weigh many pounds and allows the plant to survive years of drought or wildfire. For one night each summer, synchronized populations open huge, intensely fragrant white trumpet flowers after dark, a desert spectacle that closes forever by the following morning. Grow it tucked partly in the shade of a nurse shrub in very fast-draining soil, and water only sparingly, since the fleshy root rots quickly if kept consistently moist.

planting.note: Sow shallowly over a mineral seed mix under bright warm light; this Bolivian species germinates readily and clusters into offsets faster than many high-altitude Andean cacti.

directions: Found on the rocky slopes of the Bolivian Andes, this compact globular cactus forms dense clusters of ribbed, gray-green stems studded with prominent tubercles and short, comb-like golden-brown spines pressed close to the body. Bright golden-yellow, satin-textured flowers emerge from the woolly crown in a ring around the growing point in spring, contrasting sharply with the plant's spiny, understated body. It resembles some Rebutia and Sulcorebutia species to which it is closely related, but tends toward larger, more strongly ribbed stems and a more clustering, mounding habit over time. Provide full sun, a very gritty substrate, and a distinct dry winter rest to encourage the heaviest flowering the following spring.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Best started from rooted offsets removed from the base of a mature clump, since named color forms selected for their striking epidermis do not always come true from seed.

directions: Discovered in the mountains near Villa Serrano, Bolivia, this small clustering cactus is prized among collectors for an epidermis that shifts through unusual shades of purple, bronze, and olive-green depending on light intensity, season, and individual clone. Dense mounds of flattened, tuberculate stems are set with short, dark, comb-like spines, and in spring each head can produce multiple large magenta-pink flowers nearly as wide as the stem itself. Compared with the closely related genus Rebutia, Sulcorebutia species like this one tend to form tighter, more tuberculate clusters and show a wider range of body coloration under bright light. Grow in a very lean, fast-draining mix with bright light (some direct sun tempered by light shade to preserve the deepest coloration) and a pronounced dry winter rest.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Sow over a well-aerated mineral mix and keep warm and evenly moist until germination, then transition quickly to a drier regime, as seedlings of this nearly spineless species are prone to rot if kept wet.

directions: Discovered on cliffs in the Peruvian Andes, this diminutive globular cactus is celebrated among collectors for a body that is nearly bare of spines, leaving its smooth, blue-green skin fully exposed in a way that is unusual among the otherwise heavily armed genus Matucana. From the woolly crown emerge slender, tubular flowers in vivid red-orange that flare open at the tip, held well above the body on a curved tube. The naked-looking stem makes it far more vulnerable to sunscald and rot than its spinier relatives, so it is generally grown with some protection from the harshest midday sun rather than in fully exposed desert conditions. Use a very fast-draining mineral substrate, water sparingly even in the growing season, and keep it nearly dry and frost-free over winter.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Sow in a well-drained mix and support the sprawling stems with a stake or nearby shrub as the plant matures, since this rare Florida native scrambles rather than growing upright.

directions: One of Florida's rarest native cacti, restricted to a narrow strip of Atlantic coastal ridge scrub in Martin and St. Lucie counties, this federally endangered species sends up long, slender, gray-green stems that sprawl and lean on surrounding vegetation for support rather than standing fully erect like most columnar cacti. Its large, intensely sweet-scented white flowers open only after dark in summer and wilt by mid-morning, giving way to round, red, fleshy fruit relished by wildlife. Habitat loss to coastal development has reduced it to a handful of protected populations, making garden and botanical-collection cultivation an important conservation tool. Grow in sharply drained sandy soil in full sun, giving the lax stems something to lean against, and water only during active summer growth.

planting.note: Sow over a very open, mineral-rich mix and keep humid and warm to germinate, then grow on carefully since this small Brazilian species is one of the more exacting members of its genus in cultivation.

directions: Endemic to a small area of Minas Gerais, Brazil, this miniature member of Discocactus forms a flattened, disc-like body only a couple of inches across, ribbed and set with fine, close-lying spines that give the young plant a delicate, bristly look. Mature specimens develop a small woolly-and-bristled cephalium at the crown, a specialized flowering structure from which tiny, intensely fragrant white night-blooming flowers emerge in summer. It is one of the smallest species in a genus already known for diminutive stature, distinguishing it from larger-bodied Discocactus relatives grown more commonly in collections. Because it is markedly more sensitive to overwatering and cold than typical globular cacti, grow it in an especially fast-draining mineral mix, in bright but filtered light, and keep it warm and dry through winter dormancy.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Sow in a deep, well-drained container to accommodate the eventual taproot, and expect very slow growth for years before the columnar form becomes obvious.

directions: Native to the semi-arid highlands of Hidalgo and Queretaro in central Mexico, this tall, solitary columnar cactus is named for its unusually numerous, shallow, closely spaced ribs — often twenty or more, giving the trunk a finely pleated, almost fluted appearance compared with the fewer, bolder ribs of related Neobuxbaumia and Cephalocereus species. Young plants are densely covered in short white to yellowish spines that soften visually with age as the lower trunk grays and becomes more woody in texture. In habitat it slowly reaches well over 20 feet, though in cultivation it remains a large architectural pot or landscape specimen for many years before flowering, producing small nocturnal white flowers near the crown once mature. Grow in full sun with a coarse mineral soil and minimal winter water, protecting it from prolonged frost.

planting.note: Sow over a gritty, fast-draining mix and keep cool rather than hot, since this high-Andean species grows at elevation and resents the warm, humid conditions that suit lowland cacti.

directions: Named for the Peruvian mining town of La Oroya near which it was first collected, this globular to short-cylindrical cactus grows on rocky slopes high in the Andes along the upper Rio Santa drainage, at elevations where nights are cold even though days are bright and sunny. Densely packed ribs bear radiating clusters of stiff, often golden-brown spines that shade the body from intense high-altitude sun, and a ring of pink to magenta flowers opens near the crown in the growing season. It differs from lower-elevation Andean globular cacti such as Matucana in its more heavily ribbed, spinier body and its adaptation to a cooler, more seasonal climate. Grow in full sun with excellent drainage, moderate summer water, and a cool, nearly dry winter rest that mimics its high-altitude dormancy in habitat.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
